4. The respondent No. 1, the added respondent Nos. 2A and 2B contented the said application by filing respective affidavit-in-opposition denying material allegations set out in the petition. All these respondents although concurred to the prayer for condonation of delay for holding of the AGMs for the aforesaid years but opposed the consequential directions prayed for by the petitioner. The answering respondents in their respective affidavits-in-opposition in more or less the same terms contended that the board of directors having recommended for the 19th AGM to be held for the year 2004 and the board of directors having fixed book closure and the said date having expired, there is no scope for fixing a new record date for the said AGM in view of SEC Notification No. SEC/CMRRCD/2001-14/24/ Admin/-03 dated 26-11-2011 (Gazetted on 10-12-2001). It was further stated that fixing of record date is a matter that lies the issuer in view of section 2 (Chha) read with section 44 of the Depository (User) Regulation, 2003. The Securities and Exchange Commission also issued another Notification under section 2CC of the Securities and Exchange Ordinance, 1969 conforming that the board of directors of an issuer will fix the record date. It was contended that the fixation of record date is a legal compulsion, which is a duty assignment on the board of directors to discharge the same at the proper time when arrives and the Court may not interfere with regard to fixation of record date in a preemptive manner at a premature stage. It has further been stated by the respondent that the constitution of the Election Commission as prayed for is not permissible under Rules 15B(5), (6) and (7) of the Insurance Rules, 1958 (the said Rules). This concept is foreign to the Companies Act, 1994 as well. It is asserted by the respondents that the Rule, having spelt out the method of appointing Election Commission, this Court should not venture into the appointment of an Election Commission in contravention of the said in as much as, when no case been made out by the petitioner as to the neutrality of the chairman of the board. In the affidavit-in-opposition, it has further been stated that section 76(2) of the Insurance Act, 2010 (Insurance Act) makes it mandatory that the election of the directors shall be conducted as per the Rules prescribed. Relying on section 76(2) of Insurance Act read with Rules 15B(5), (6) and (7) of the said Rules the respondents contended that the prayer for independent election commission is barred. 

 38. Referring to Rule 15B(1) Mr Karim submitted that Rule 15B(1) provides that the holders of public subscription shares shall elect the directors under Rule 15A. Mr Karim submits that Rule 15A provides the qualification of public subscriber directors. Relying on Rule 15B(1) Mr Karim submitted that under Rule 15B(1) only the public share-holders shall elect a public subscriber as a director. Mr Karim submits that Rule 15B(1) does not permit a sponsor share-holder to elect a public subscribed director. So under Rule 15B(1) sponsor share-holders cannot elect public directors. According to Mr Karim since sponsor share-holders cannot elect public directors under Rule 15B it will be a discriminatory treatment if the public share-holders are allowed to elect sponsor directors in as much as Rule 15B(1) does not speak that the public holders of public subscription shares shall elect sponsor share-holders. As a result Article 96 is fully in consonance with Rule 15B of the Insurance Rules, 1958. Therefore, the contention of the petitioner in Matter No. 61 of 2010 that the share-holders irrespective of their classes shall indiscriminately vote for both sponsor directors and public directors in two separate ballots is misconceived. 

 66. Though, it is difficult to give a legal definition of "promoters/ sponsor share-holders" as a general principle of law applicable to all instance irrespective of differential facts and circumstances, but it is not practically impossible for the respondent No. 1 company to ascertain as to who are "promoters/ sponsor share-holders" in the instant case. As I have already found that there are two groups of share-holders namely sponsor share-holders and public subscribers. So sponsor share-holders are those members of the company who are not public subscribers. The relevant Insurance Act required that 50% of the shares to be subscribed by the public and 50% of shares to be subscribed by the sponsors. So those who become member of the respondent No. 1 company by way of subscribing the said 50% shares reserved for the public are public subscribers and rest of the members of the company are sponsor share-holders. Section 3(2) of the Capital Issues (Continuance of Control) Act, 1947 (as then was in force) required that a company must obtain consent of the Government for making any public offer of securities. Further section 4 of the said Capital Issues (Continuance of Control) Act, 1947 (as then was in force) also required the respondent No. 1 company to issue prospectus offering for subscription or publicly offering for sale securities stating that it has obtained consent of the Government. Under the provision of said Capital Issues (Continuance of Control) Act, 1947 (as then was in force), the Government vide Memo No. MF/ Inv-42/86/508 dated 02-11-1986 accorded its consent to public offer to the extent of 50% shares of the respondent No. 1 company. Relevant part of the said consent of Government dated 1-11-1986 runs as follows:— 

 70. Section 76(1) gives right to the share-holders. This right is not attached to shares. The promoters have right to elect 12 directors in the board. Promoters are those who have originally subscribed to the memorandum and Articles of Association. So promoters or sponsors are the original share-holders, who floated the company by way of subscribing to the memorandum and Articles of Association named therein. If the promoters transfer their shares then the transferee does not become promoters or sponsor share-holders. This right is a right in personam. This right can be enjoyed by the promoters so long they remain as member of the company. Section 76(2) provides that share-holders shall elect directors in the manner prescribed by the rules framed under the Insurance Act, 2010. The Insurance Rules, 1958 is deemed to be the Rules framed under the Insurance Act, 2010. I shall discuss the manner prescribed by Rules, 1958 later. Before that, I shall consult the Articles of Association of the company attaching any right, if any, to the said two classes of share-holders namely sponsor share-holder and public subscribers in respect of electing sponsor directors and public directors respectively. 

 73. Section 76(2) of the Insurance Act, 2010 provides that directors shall be elected in the manner prescribed in the Rules. The Insurance Rules, 1958 is deemed to be Rules framed under the Insurance Act, 2010 in view of section 160(2)(q) of the Insurance Act, 2010. Rule 15A and Rule 15B of the Insurance Rules, 1958 provides the manner for election of directors by public subscribers. The Insurance Rules, 1958 does not provide any thing for electing directors representing sponsor share-holders. Rule 15B(1) of the Insurance Rules, 1958 confines the public subscribers to elect the directors representing public subscribers. Rule 15B(1) of the Insurance Rules, 1958 states as follows:— 

 74. Dr Zahir, the learned Counsel argued that in view of Rule 15B(1) of the Insurance Rules, 1958 public subscribers shall elect directors representing public subscribers as well as the directors representing sponsor share-holder, but sponsor share-holders shall not be eligible to elect directors representing public subscribers. I find it difficult to agree with the submissions made by Dr Zahir Rules 15B(1) does not speak that public subscribers shall also elect directors representing sponsor share-holders. Rule 15B(1) simply provides that public subscribers shall elect directors representing public subscribers. This means that the right of public subscribers to elect directors is confined to the election of directors representing the public subscribers. So the public subscribers cannot exercise their right of election beyond directors representing public subscribers i.e. they cannot elect directors representing sponsor share-holders. Rule 15B(1) not only exclude all other share-holders (i.e. sponsor share-holders) other than public subscribers to elect director representing public subscribers, but the said Rule 15B(1) in the same vein is restrictive clause upon public subscribers in electing directors representing public subscribers only. If the legislature had the intention only to debar the sponsor share-holders in participating election of directors representing public subscribers then the legislature would provide in the plain language to that effect stating that in clear language that the sponsor share-holders shall not be eligible to participate in electing directors representing public subscribers. So I am fully convinced that Rule 15B(1) completely attached rights to public subscribers to elect only directors representing public subscribers and also by necessary implication debars the public subscribers to participate in electing sponsor directors and also debars sponsor share-holders in electing public directors. 

 86. I also do not find that the prospectus issued by the company operate as estoppel in respect of the issues specifically provided in Articles of Association. Documents which are deposited with a statutory or Government agency in compliance of law of the land, moreso if the public have access to the same, then the said document being in public domain are public documents. Articles of Association of a company is also a public document. Dr Zahir argued that prospectus provides that each share will have one voting right and since it does not prove that voting right will be limited to the effect that the holders of public shares will not be able to cast vote for election for sponsors-directors, the prospectus operates as estoppel upon the company to allow public subscriber to cast vote for election of sponsor-directors. This submission does not hold good since Articles of Association being a public document such omission in the prospectus to the effect as argued cannot operate as estoppel. Moreover, Articles of Association was part of the prospectus and therefore, the classification of share-holders with restriction as aforesaid was in disclosure procedure. So I find no substance in this submission. In this respect, Clause 20 of the Schedule 3 of the Companies Act, 1994 stipulates that the information as to restriction or privileges regarding voting of the members of the company must be stipulated in the prospectus. This Clause 20 manifestly shows that the Companies Act, 1994 recognizes classification of share-holders in terms of voting power. However, in failing to mentioning the same in the prospectus the provisions of the Companies Act, 1994 such as section 145 stipulates the consequences of civil liabilities and other. But the Companies Act, 1994 nowhere provide that for failing to mentioning the same, the terms of the Articles of Association of any company shall be invalidated. As such I find no substance in the argument of Dr Zahir failure to mentioning the classification of share-holders invalidate the right of the share-holders as to voting power.
